 Order

The accused in C.C.No.518 of 1997 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class,
Mavelikara, filed this revision petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2 (ia) (m), 7 (i) and 16 (1) (a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Section 16 (1) (a) (ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 r/w Rule 50 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955.

entities.text:
Judicial Magistrate of First Class,
Mavelikara
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Heard.
3.
The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 25.10.1996 at about 11.00 p.m., PW1, the Food Inspector purchased 750 gram of coriander from the accused.
After sampling as per rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis.
After analysis, the Public Analyst submitted Ext.P12 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for coriander and was therefore adulterated.

Thereafter, on the request of the accused,
the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis.

Ext.P20 certificate of analysis would also show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for the food item as per the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and was therefore adulterated.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW3 were examined and Exts.P1 to P20 were marked for the prosecution.
No evidence was marked on the side of the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext.P20 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee)
and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P20 certificate of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in K.Rajan vs State Of Kerala on 3 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/186936744/
2

entities.text: K.Rajan vs State Of Kerala on 3 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Pepsico
India Holdings (supra)

. It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra)
that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico India Holdings (supra), the conviction in this case under Sections 2 (ia) (m), 7 (i) and 16 (1) (a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

For the above said reasons, the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2 (ia) (m), 7 (i) and 16 (1) (a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act,
1954 stand set aside and the revision petitioner is acquitted for the said offence.
7. The courts below concurrently found that the revision petitioner sold the food item without having a valid licence under the PFA Rules.
There is no material before the court to indicate that the revision petitioner had a valid licence under the PFA Rules during the relevant period to sell the food item.

Having gone through the relevant inputs, I find no reason to interference with the concurrent finding by the courts below that the revision petitioner sold the food item without having a valid licence under the PFA Rules.

Therefore, the conviction passed by the courts below under Section 16 (1)
(a) (ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act r/w Rule 50 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, does not warrant any interference by this Court.
8. As regards the sentence, the learned counsel for the revision petitioner has pleaded for leniency.
There is no previous conviction against the revision petitioner.

Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the view that the revision petitioner can be sentenced under the second proviso to Section 16 (1) of the PFA Act and accordingly, the revision petitioner is sentenced to imprisonment till the rising of the court and a fine of Rs.500/- (Rupees five hundred only) and in default to simple imprisonment for five days under Section 16 (1) (a) (ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act r/w Rule 50 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, to meet the ends of Justice.
In the result, this revision petition stands allowed in part as above.
The revision petitioner shall surrender before the trial court on 26.04.2016 to suffer the sentence.

Sd/-
B. SUDHEENDRA KUMAR JUDGE Scl/03.03.2016
